title: WNT/β-catenin signaling: implications for homeostasis and tumorigenesis in the esophagus
abstract: The WNT/β-catenin signaling pathway plays a central role in the development, homeostasis, and tumorigenesis of the gastrointestinal tract. During embryonic development, dynamic regulation of β-catenin activity is essential for foregut formation and for the transition of the esophageal epithelium from columnar to stratified squamous morphology, with inhibitory signals ensuring proper lineage specification. In the adult esophagus, however, the precise role of WNT/β-catenin signaling in basal progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation remains incompletely understood, although dysregulation of this pathway, including overexpression of WNT ligands and downregulation of WNT inhibitors, has been observed in Barrett's esophagus (BE) and esophageal cancer. This review highlights recent insights into the roles of WNT signaling in esophageal development, epithelial homeostasis, and disease pathogenesis.

title: Radiotherapy-induced PD-L1 conversion in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: From multidimensional mechanisms to clinical rescue strategies
abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) remains a formidable malignancy, with patients harboring programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1)-negative tumors frequently exhibiting an "immune desert" phenotype and poor response to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Radiotherapy (RT), traditionally utilized for localized cytoreduction, acts as an in situ vaccine capable of remodeling the tumor immune microenvironment. A potential contributor to RT-ICB synergy is RT-associated modulation of PD-L1 expression, including possible conversion from a PD-L1-negative to a PD-L1-positive state. This review synthesizes ESCC-specific evidence and cross-tumor mechanistic data regarding cGAS-STING-mediated DNA sensing, eIF2α/ATF4-driven translational stress, epigenetic de-repression, metabolic-stromal signaling, and vesicular PD-L1 dissemination. While RT-induced PD-L1 upregulation serves as an adaptive resistance mechanism that can be therapeutically exploited, significant clinical barriers remain. Notable challenges include radiation-induced lymphopenia and overlapping toxicities, despite high pathological complete response rates in recent neoadjuvant RT-ICB trials. To address the needs of the PD-L1-negative population, we evaluate current clinical evidence and ongoing trial strategies. We emphasize the need to refine, rather than replace, existing radiotherapy paradigms through precision-oriented strategies, including careful optimization of spatiotemporal sequencing, cautious exploration of immunomodulatory low-dose radiotherapy, and structural preservation approaches such as tumor-draining lymph node sparing. By modulating stromal and metabolic resistance through refined RT parameters, localized radiation may be effectively translated into durable, systemic antitumor immunity.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Tertiary lymphoid structures for anti-tumor immunotherapy
abstract: Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) are transient ectopic lymphoid-like structures potentiating the adaptive anti-tumor immunotherapy efficiency. They have been observed across diverse malignancies since they were initially found to correlate with favorable prognosis in non-small cell lung cancer. Importantly, TLSs could systematically enhance immune responses efficiency by optimizing the immune ecology of the tumor microenvironment (TME). They have attracted considerable interest as predictive biomarkers for anti-tumor treatment responses, including immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and potential chemotherapy. However, TLSs formation within tumor is poorly controllable, and lacks effective strategies for precisely modulating their formation and function. In this comprehensive review, we first summarize the composition and formation mechanism of TLSs. Second, we address the role of TLSs in enhancing anti-tumor immunotherapy efficiency. Third, we explore the advanced methods to modulate TLSs formation. Finally, we summarize novel multifunctional materials for facilitating TLSs formation to enhance anti-tumor immunotherapy both in basic research and clinical applications. Deep understanding of the formation mechanism and role of TLSs could provide insights into modulation of TLSs for improving anti-tumor immunotherapy efficiency.

title: Targeting extracellular vesicle-mediated tumor-immune symbiosis: From molecular mechanisms to translational implications
abstract: Symbiotic interactions between tumor cells and immune cells are key drivers of tumor progression and treatment resistance. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are key mediators of intercellular crosstalk within the tumor microenvironment. An increasing number of studies have demonstrated that EVs play a significant role in regulating tumor-immune symbiosis. Tumor cell-derived EVs can modulate the function of various immune cells within the microenvironment, mediating immune suppression and promoting tumor growth. Correspondingly, immune cells also produce EVs that promote malignant phenotypes in tumor cells, such as proliferation, invasion, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and treatment resistance. Targeting EV-mediated tumor-immune symbiosis has emerged as a promising strategy in cancer therapy. In this review, we introduce the biogenesis and heterogeneity of EVs, highlighting the bidirectional pro-tumoral crosstalk between tumor cells and immune cells. Furthermore, we summarize current therapeutic strategies targeting EVs to break tumor-immune symbiosis and offer perspectives on future directions in this advancing field.

title: Ubiquitination in DNA double-strand break repair: Mechanisms, regulation, and therapeutic implications
abstract: DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair depends on tightly coordinated signaling that controls damage recognition, chromatin remodeling, pathway choice, and repair termination. Among the regulatory layers involved, ubiquitination functions as a central organizing axis of the DNA damage response (DDR), directing the ordered assembly, retention, and turnover of repair factors at damaged chromatin. The RNF8-RNF168 ubiquitin cascade represents a core signaling module that amplifies DSB signals and licenses downstream repair programs. In this review, we summarize recent advances in ubiquitin-dependent regulation of DSB repair, focusing on how ubiquitination governs repair factor dynamics and the balance between classical non-homologous end joining (cNHEJ) and homologous recombination (HR). We further discuss SUMO modification as a tightly coupled regulatory layer that cooperates with ubiquitin signaling to fine-tune signal amplitude and duration through coordinated SUMO-ubiquitin interactions and SUMO-targeted ubiquitination. In addition to ubiquitin-centered regulation, emerging crosstalk with phosphorylation, methylation, acetylation, and PARylation further shapes repair timing, pathway commitment, and signal resolution. Finally, we discuss the translational implications of ubiquitin- and SUMO-centered DDR regulation, highlighting how adaptive repair states and acquired resistance to genotoxic therapies create exploitable therapeutic vulnerabilities.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: The cGAS-STING signaling in hepatocellular carcinoma: A spatiotemporally gated immune switch linking pro-tumorigenic immune evasion and anti-tumor therapeutic response
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) arises from chronic inflammation and immune tolerance, posing substantial challenges for immunotherapy. The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling is a central immunological hub linking innate immune sensing to adaptive immune responses in tumors. In HCC, cGAS-STING signaling exhibits a context-dependent dual role across multiple hepatic cell types, including hepatocytes, hepatic stellate cells and immune cells, orchestrating both anti-tumor immunity and pro-tumorigenic inflammation. While acute activation enhances dendritic cell maturation, antigen presentation, and CD8+ T-cell priming to boost anti-tumor immunity, sustained or dysregulated cGAS-STING signaling promotes chronic inflammation and subsequently remodels an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) to promote tumorigenesis. This dual functionality positions the cGAS-STING signaling as both a therapeutic opportunity and a critical constraint in HCC immunotherapy. Recent advances highlight the translational potential of STING-targeted strategies, including synthetic agonists, combination regimens with targeted therapies, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) as well as nanomaterial-based delivery systems. At the same time, clinical translation remains constrained by systemic inflammatory toxicity, context-dependent tumor-promoting inflammation, pathway refractoriness or silencing, and the lack of validated biomarkers for patient selection. In this review, we summarize the molecular mechanisms, cell-type-specific functions and intercellular crosstalk of cGAS-STING signaling in HCC, and discuss therapeutic strategies and translational challenges. We propose future directions focusing on spatiotemporal activation, precision delivery, and biomarker-guided interventions to exploit the therapeutic potential of targeting the cGAS-STING signaling in HCC.

title: Macrophage-mesenchymal crosstalk in recurrent glioblastoma: a perspective for therapeutic strategies
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most lethal cancers, with recurrence in nearly all patients despite standard therapy. However, the biological mechanisms governing recurrence remain incompletely understood. Increasing evidence suggests that recurrence is driven not only by tumor-intrinsic resistance, but also by dynamic reciprocal interactions between tumor cell plasticity and the tumor microenvironment (TME). Here, we integrate these dynamic interactions into a unifying ecological framework in which therapeutic stress induces proneural-to-mesenchymal transition (PMT), a phenotypic shift associated with increased invasiveness, inflammatory signaling, and treatment tolerance. Mesenchymal tumor states remodel the TME by promoting the recruitment and functional reprogramming of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs), which become increasingly enriched in recurrent tumors. In turn, macrophage-derived cytokines, including IL-6 and TGF-β, together with metabolites such as lactate and cholesterol derivatives, reinforce mesenchymal transcriptional programs and stabilize tumor cell states through immunometabolic interactions. We highlight how this bidirectional crosstalk forms a macrophage-mesenchymal feedback loop that sustains the recurrent tumor ecosystem. Fundamentally metabolism acts as a key regulatory layer that links immune polarization to tumor cell plasticity. Finally, we outline therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting this circuit, emphasizing combination approaches that concurrently target phenotypic plasticity, macrophage recruitment and function, and metabolic crosstalk. A circuit-informed perspective provides a conceptual basis for designing more effective interventions against recurrent GBM.

title: The endothelial cell–neutrophil axis: Mechanisms and therapeutic perspectives in colitis-associated carcinogenesis
abstract: Endothelial dysfunction coupled with neutrophil infiltration drives colitis-associated carcinogenesis (CAC). Vascular endothelial cells sustain homeostasis and immune surveillance. In CAC, endothelial impairment increases vascular permeability, recruits neutrophils, aggravates inflammation, and further stimulates angiogenesis, thereby promoting tumor proliferation and metastasis. Targeting endothelial signaling cascades, including the VEGF and MAPK axes, represents a promising strategy for suppressing inflammatory responses and tumor outgrowth. Blockade of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 and ICAM-1 curtails neutrophil recruitment and mitigates intestinal inflammatory lesions. Anti-VEGF and MAPK-targeted interventions have been investigated in cancer and inflammatory diseases, and emerging work on neutrophil extracellular traps opens new therapeutic directions. Despite these mechanistic and translational advances, a systematic overview of the interplay between endothelial cells and neutrophils during CAC remains lacking. Here we describe the central contribution of endothelial dysfunction to the multistep progression of CAC, discuss how therapeutic modulation of the endothelial cell-neutrophil axis could optimize clinical outcomes, and highlight vascular endothelium-targeted interventions as promising strategies for limiting CAC progression.

title: Lysine specific demethylase 5B promises to be a new focus of cancer drug-resistance: combination therapy
abstract: Drug resistance remains a major obstacle to the long-term efficacy of cancer therapy. Lysine specific demethylase 5B (KDM5B), an epigenetic regulator of H3K4 methylation, has emerged as an important modulator of therapeutic resistance across multiple tumor contexts. In this review, we systematically summarize the mechanisms through which KDM5B contributes to drug resistance, including DNA damage repair, replication stress adaptation, cellular-state plasticity, pro-survival signaling, metabolic reprogramming, and immune regulation. Importantly, the available evidence indicates that KDM5B functions through both catalytic-dependent and catalytic-independent mechanisms, and that the relative contribution of these functions varies according to tumor type, treatment pressure, and cellular context. We further highlight two emerging immunoregulatory mechanisms involving KDM5B-mediated suppression of the cGAS-STING pathway and demethylase-independent cooperation with SETDB1, while distinguishing mechanistic rationale from experimentally validated combination strategies. Building on these findings, we discuss mechanism-guided combination approaches, including catalytic inhibition, protein degradation, disruption of protein-protein interactions, and combinations with DNA-damaging agents, targeted therapies, and immunotherapies. We also summarize candidate biomarkers for patient stratification and discuss major translational challenges, including target selectivity, tumor heterogeneity, pharmacological limitations, and acquired resistance. Collectively, this review provides a context- and mechanism-guided framework for understanding KDM5B-mediated drug resistance and for developing biomarker-informed combination strategies. Clinical trial number: not applicable.

title: Lipid metabolic regulation and targeting strategies in the brain metastasis tumor microenvironment
abstract: Brain metastasis is a major contributor to poor prognosis in cancer patients, with therapeutic efficacy severely constrained by the blood-brain barrier and the complex brain microenvironment. Although lipid metabolic reprogramming has been linked to tumor progression across multiple cancer types, its mechanistic involvement in brain metastasis, particularly its reciprocal interactions with central nervous system microenvironmental cells, remains insufficiently defined. This review synthesizes existing evidence to elucidate how lipid metabolic reprogramming promotes tumor cell colonization and growth in the brain and to evaluate its therapeutic relevance. Current findings indicate that metastatic tumor cells adapt to the brain microenvironment via increased de novo lipogenesis, altered cholesterol metabolism, reduced fatty acid oxidation, and enhanced uptake of exogenous lipids. Emerging evidence further indicates reciprocal lipid-metabolic interactions between metastatic tumor cells and central nervous system-resident cells; however, the directionality, cell-type specificity, and underlying molecular mechanisms of this metabolic crosstalk remain insufficiently characterized. Such interactions may promote immunosuppressive microenvironmental remodeling and facilitate metastatic progression. Significant heterogeneity is observed among primary tumor types in their use of lipid metabolism associated mechanisms. Targeting critical nodes at the interface of lipid metabolic reprogramming and microenvironmental interactions may therefore help overcome current therapeutic limitations in brain metastasis. Future studies using advanced multi-omics approaches are expected to define spatial heterogeneity and support the development of combination strategies capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier, ultimately informing improved clinical management strategies.

title: Metabolic reprogramming and plasticity in breast Cancer: Mechanisms driving tumor progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance
abstract: Breast cancer remains the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. Despite substantial advances in endocrine therapy, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy, therapeutic resistance and metastatic progression remain major clinical challenges. Accumulating evidence has established metabolic reprogramming as a fundamental hallmark of breast cancer, enabling tumor cells to adapt dynamically to nutrient limitation, hypoxia, oxidative stress, and therapeutic pressure. Beyond the classical Warburg effect, breast cancer cells exhibit remarkable metabolic plasticity through coordinated reprogramming of glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), glutamine metabolism, lipid metabolism, and one‑carbon metabolism. These metabolic alterations not only sustain bioenergetic and biosynthetic demands but also reshape the tumor microenvironment (TME), promote immune evasion, maintain cancer stemness, and facilitate metastatic dissemination. Recent studies further reveal that metabolic heterogeneity varies substantially across molecular subtypes, metastatic niches, and treatment-resistant cell populations. In parallel, stromal cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), and immune cells establish complex metabolic symbiotic relationships with tumor cells through metabolite exchange and immunometabolic regulation. Importantly, therapy-induced metabolic adaptation has emerged as a central mechanism underlying resistance to chemotherapy, endocrine therapy, HER2-targeted therapy, CDK4/6 inhibitors, and immune checkpoint blockade. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the molecular mechanisms governing metabolic reprogramming and metabolic plasticity in breast cancer, with particular emphasis on how they contribute to tumor progression, metastasis, immune escape, and therapeutic resistance. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies targeting glycolysis, mitochondrial metabolism, glutamine utilization, lipid metabolism, ferroptosis-associated pathways, and immunometabolic vulnerabilities. Finally, we highlight current challenges in clinical translation, including metabolic heterogeneity, compensatory pathway activation, and limited therapeutic selectivity, and outline future directions that integrate multi-omics profiling, spatial metabolomics, and precision metabolic targeting for individualized breast cancer therapy.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: From recognition to serial killing: Molecular mechanisms controlling NK-cell-mediated tumor elimination
abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells are critical regulators of tumor immune surveillance and represent an important platform for cancer immunotherapy. However, the ability of NK cells to eliminate tumor cells is determined by a multistep cellular process involving signal integration, cytotoxic interface formation, effector execution, and functional maintenance. Conventional evaluation approaches, including receptor-ligand profiling, cytokine production, CD107a degranulation and endpoint cytotoxicity assays, provide valuable measurements of overall NK activity but often fail to define the specific cellular process that limits tumor-cell elimination. Here, we propose a stage-resolved framework to interpret NK-cell antitumor cytotoxicity by dividing the killing process into four interconnected functional stages: recognition and early activation, cytotoxic synapse maturation, effector delivery and death execution, and serial killing with sustained tumor control. For each stage, we summarize the molecular mechanisms that regulate signal initiation, receptor organization, cytoskeletal remodeling, granule trafficking, target-cell death sensitivity, and metabolic adaptation. We further discuss how tumor-intrinsic resistance programs and therapeutic interventions influence individual stages of the NK-cell killing process. This framework provides a mechanistic perspective for understanding heterogeneous NK-cell dysfunction by localizing functional constraints within the cytotoxic cascade rather than relying solely on global activity measurements. By linking molecular mechanisms with stage-specific functional readouts, this approach may facilitate the identification of actionable targets, interpretation of therapeutic responses, and rational development of combination strategies in NK-cell-based cancer immunotherapy.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Glycosylation in colorectal cancer: From tumor-intrinsic signaling to the host–microbiome glyco-interface
abstract: Aberrant glycosylation is increasingly recognized as a key regulatory layer in colorectal cancer (CRC), extending beyond tumor-cell-intrinsic signaling to shape the tumor microenvironment and host-microbiome interactions. In the immune compartment, glycosylation modulates the stability and activity of classical checkpoints, including PD-L1, while tumor-associated glycans engage MGL, DC-SIGN, Siglecs, and galectins to form glyco-immune checkpoints that influence T-cell dysfunction, macrophage polarization, dendritic-cell tolerance, and NK-cell activity. These mechanisms support emerging glyco-immunotherapeutic strategies such as targeted desialylation, glycoform-specific targeting, and combination with immune checkpoint blockade. Glycosylation also functions as a molecular language at the host-microbiome interface. Site-specific epithelial glycoproteins, mucin O-glycoforms, bidirectional host-bacterial fucosylation, IgA-associated glycan recognition, and microbial glycan utilization may collectively shape CRC-associated dysbiosis and mucosal inflammation. Integrating stool glycoproteomics with microbiome profiling may further enable noninvasive screening and patient stratification. This review highlights glycosylation as a multidimensional interface linking tumor biology, antitumor immunity, and microbiome ecology, with implications for biomarker development and precision therapy in CRC.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Beyond the membrane: lipid rafts and oxysterols establish cholesterol as a dynamic signaling hub while underlying the cholesterol paradox in cancer
abstract: Metabolic reprogramming of cholesterol extends beyond its canonical role in membrane biogenesis, serving as a dynamic signaling hub that facilitates tumor progression and therapy resistance. In cancer therapy, the limited clinical efficacy and variable outcomes of non-selective lipid-lowering interventions, such as statins, underscore an incomplete understanding of these underlying regulatory networks. This review addresses the paradoxical roles of cholesterol in oncology, in which cancer cells leverage oxysterols and membrane lipid rafts to promote metastasis, immunosuppression, and therapy resistance, while baseline cholesterol homeostasis remains essential for proper immune cell function. We review the initiation of cholesterol metabolic reprogramming and evaluate the resulting metabolic conflict. Furthermore, we examine how immune cells adapt metabolically to cholesterol competition within the tumor microenvironment (TME), the role of cholesterol in pre-metastatic niche formation and organotropism, and its involvement in drug resistance through efflux transporters and ferroptosis suppression. These mechanistic insights may inform the rationale for targeted metabolic therapeutic strategies.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Lipid metabolic reprogramming in Cancer radiation resistance: Mechanisms and therapeutic implications
abstract: Currently, cancer treatment mainly includes surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy, wherein radiotherapy is one of the core modalities. However, its efficacy is often limited by radiotherapy resistance in the tumour cells. In recent years, studies have found that tumour cells undergo lipid metabolic reprogramming to enhance lipid synthesis, uptake, and storage, thereby adapting to the energy and structural adjustment demands imposed by radiotherapy, gaining survival advantage and developing radiation resistance. This review mainly focused on the role of lipid metabolic changes, including fatty acids, cholesterol, and phospholipids, in radiation resistance, aiming to provide ideas for achieving individualised precision radiotherapy.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Beyond target presence: A cross-cancer contextual framework for siRNA therapeutics in solid tumors
abstract: Small interfering RNA (siRNA) has achieved clinical success in liver-directed therapies, but its translation to solid tumors remains limited by heterogeneous delivery and context-dependent target dependence. This review compares non-small cell lung cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, breast cancer, glioblastoma, and hepatocellular carcinoma across four interconnected dimensions: resistance networks, tumor microenvironmental reprogramming, metastatic progression, and delivery-system design. We examine how bypass signaling and phenotypic plasticity influence target selection, how stromal and immune compartments shape therapeutic responses, and how disease stage and organ-specific barriers alter delivery requirements. We then assess representative clinical RNA interference programs to distinguish evidence of tissue exposure and target engagement from antitumor activity and established clinical benefit. Across these settings, tumor accumulation does not establish productive cytosolic delivery, and target knockdown alone does not ensure durable disease control. We propose a context-dependent framework that aligns functional target dependence with the intended cell population, tissue environment, treatment timing, and delivery route. Priorities include resistance-informed combinations, prospective validation of delivery biomarkers, repeat-dose safety assessment, and carrier designs whose functional benefits justify their manufacturing complexity. By linking mechanistic comparison with clinical evidence, this review identifies testable criteria for selecting patients, evaluating functional delivery, and advancing siRNA therapeutics for solid tumors.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Molecular landscape of chondrosarcoma: From tumor biology to therapeutic vulnerabilities
abstract: Chondrosarcoma (CS) is the second most common primary malignant bone tumor and comprises a heterogeneous group of cartilage-producing neoplasms with distinct histopathological, molecular, and clinical features. Surgery remains the cornerstone of treatment, whereas intrinsic resistance to conventional chemotherapy and radiotherapy limits therapeutic options for patients with unresectable or metastatic disease. This narrative review critically examines the molecular, genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and microenvironmental mechanisms underlying CS development, progression, and treatment resistance and evaluates their translational implications. CS subtypes are associated with characteristic molecular alterations, including IDH1/2 mutations in central conventional CS, EXT1/2 disruption in secondary peripheral CS, and HEY1::NCOA2 fusion in mesenchymal CS. Additional alterations involving TP53, CDKN2A/RB1, and the TERT promoter contribute to disease progression. These events interact with dysregulated signaling pathways, metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, hypoxia, extracellular-matrix remodeling, bone remodeling, and heterogeneous immune states. This biological complexity has prompted the investigation of mutant-IDH inhibitors, death receptor agonists, antiangiogenic and multitarget kinase inhibitors, immune-checkpoint blockade, and therapies targeting cell-cycle, epigenetic, metabolic, and microenvironmental dependencies. Nevertheless, most approaches have produced limited or predominantly cytostatic activity. Ozekibart has provided a positive randomized signal, with improved progression-free survival in conventional CS, whereas mutant-IDH1 inhibitors can achieve durable disease stabilization in selected patients but rarely induce objective responses. Future progress requires subtype-specific trials, assessment of pretreatment tumor growth kinetics, pharmacodynamic confirmation of target inhibition, and prospective integration of genomic, epigenetic, metabolic, and immune biomarkers.
journal_title: Biochimica et Biophysica Acta (BBA) - Reviews on Cancer

title: Dynamic changes in the metabolic network and signalling pathways of cancer stem cells in therapy resistance
abstract: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) play a pivotal role in therapeutic resistance, metastasis, and tumour recurrence. During treatment, these cells undergo dynamic changes that enable survival and metabolic adaptation, leading to poor clinical outcomes. CSCs are capable of developing resistance to drugs by alterations in metabolic and signalling pathways. They exhibit metabolic adaptations that enable therapy resistance, tumour recurrence, and metastasis. These adaptations involve shifts in glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), lipid and amino acid metabolism, mitochondrial dynamics, and interactions with the tumour microenvironment to support energy production. Depending on the biological contexts and the energy needs, CSCs can switch to different metabolic phenotypes. CSCs drive energy production and biogenesis via glycolysis in hypoxic conditions. OXPHOS is essential for sustaining cell dormancy, survival and carcinogenesis. In addition to glycolysis and OXPHOS, CSCs employ lipid metabolism for energy production via fatty acid oxidation and amino acid metabolism via glutamine metabolism, promoting redox balancing and epigenetic modifications. Taken together, this metabolic plasticity facilitates CSC survival and treatment resistance. Besides, CSCs are capable of metabolically rewiring their niche to evade apoptosis, enhance DNA repair, and promote immune evasion, which are considered hallmarks of drug resistance and cancer relapse. An in-depth understanding of the metabolic network and signalling pathways of CSCs may help in developing combination or targeted therapies against them, thereby increasing the potential to formulate effective treatment approaches for the complete eradication of cancer/CSCs. This review addresses dynamic changes in the CSCs' metabolism and signalling leading to the development of a drug-resistance phenotype, causing survival and relapse in the tumours. Therapeutic strategies targeting CSC metabolism and signalling via metabolic modulators and stemness inhibitors were discussed. Overall, CSC metabolic adaptation promotes drug resistance and tumour proliferation. Hence, targeting these metabolic adaptations offers a new perspective for the elimination of CSCs and enhanced therapy.

title: Targeting metabolic cell death in cancer to reverse drug resistance
abstract: Evasion of apoptosis is a typical feature of malignant tumors developing to survive therapeutic stress. As a result, chemotherapeutic drugs that primarily induce apoptosis can no longer effectively kill tumor cells, which brings challenges to clinical cancer treatment. Recent evidence indicates that targeting key nodes in cellular metabolic pathways can bypass apoptotic routes and induce metabolic cell death in tumor cells to overcome drug resistance. Different from the traditional ways of defining cell death that rely on morphological features, metabolic cell death focuses more on the inducing factors and the associated dysregulation of cellular metabolic pathways. Metabolic cell death can be classified into four categories based on the driver factors of cell death: (1) metal ion dyshomeostasis-mediated cell death; (2) redox-collapse cell death; (3) pH dyshomeostasis-driven cell death; and (4) metabolic byproduct accumulation-mediated cell death. According to these metabolic cell death patterns, several therapeutic strategies targeting the metabolic vulnerabilities have attracted considerable attention. Here, we summarize the major metabolic cell death patterns of tumor cells, examine how these death modalities engage anti-tumor immunity, and discuss how exploiting them can reverse drug resistance. We further discuss the therapeutic window, tumor metabolic heterogeneity, and metabolic network therapeutic implications.

title: Endothelial dysfunction in cancer: A neglected frontier in anticancer therapy
abstract: Although endothelial dysfunction (ED) is a hallmark of cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), it is also being increasingly recognised as a key contributor to cancer pathophysiology and a determinant of the cardiovascular response to anticancer therapy. Dysfunctional endothelial cells in primary tumours and metastatic organs play a critical role in cancer cell intravasation and extravasation, whereas systemic ED in patients with cancer drives CVDs. Nevertheless, anticancer therapies, such as conventional chemotherapy, kinase inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and antibody-drug conjugates, drive cancer therapy-related ED (CTR-ED) and thus contribute to cancer therapy-related cardiovascular toxicity (CTR-CVT). In contrast, major CVD therapies such as statins, renin-angiotensin system inhibitors, and sodium-glucose co-transporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve endothelial function. It is now evident that the opposite effects of CVD and cancer therapies on endothelial function-improving or worsening it, respectively-have critical therapeutic implications. Therefore, this narrative review provides an integrated pathophysiological perspective on ED in cancer, highlighting endothelial cells as a key pathophysiological component of the tumour microenvironment, metastatic organ, and systemic circulation involved in the regulation of primary tumour angiogenesis, metastasis, and systemic inflammation, as well as contributing to CTR-CVT, thus highlighting ED as a determinant of therapeutic outcomes in oncology. Nevertheless, ED, and particularly CTR-ED, represents a neglected frontier in anticancer therapy, calling for a paradigm shift toward endothelium-safe and vasoprotective treatment strategies in cancer care.

title: Gallbladder cancer beyond genetics: tumor–immune microenvironment interactions and emerging translational therapeutic strategies
abstract: Gallbladder cancer (GBC) is an aggressive malignancy where tumor-intrinsic genomic alterations fail to fully explain its rapid invasiveness and therapeutic resistance. Unlike more generic reviews focused broadly on biliary tract cancers or limited to isolated genomic profiling, this review provides an in-depth dissection of the GBC tumor microenvironment (TME) as an integrated tumor-immune-stromal-neural ecosystem. Key microenvironmental drivers are illuminated, including cancer-associated fibroblast remodeling, immunosuppressive myeloid reprogramming, T-cell dysfunction, and neuro-tumor crosstalk driving perineural invasion. Crucially, this review establishes a structured evidence hierarchy that rigorously distinguishes GBC-specific findings from broader biliary cohorts and tumor-agnostic data. By synthesizing multimodal computational frameworks and microenvironment-directed combination strategies, this review provides an actionable precision oncology roadmap to overcome therapeutic resistance and improve patient outcomes in GBC.

title: Neoantigen evolution in cancer: immunoediting, immune escape, and future vaccine strategies
abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has changed cancer treatment, with neoantigen-based vaccines emerging as a promising strategy to induce tumor-specific immune responses while minimizing adverse effects on healthy tissues. Advances in next-generation sequencing, immunopeptidomics, artificial intelligence, and computational prediction have accelerated the identification of patient-specific neoantigens and enabled the development of personalized cancer vaccines. Despite encouraging safety profiles and robust induction of neoantigen-specific T-cell responses, clinical efficacy has remained inconsistent. Tumor evolution driven by genomic instability continuously reshapes the neoantigen landscape through intratumoral heterogeneity, immune-mediated selection, and antigen gain or loss, facilitating immune escape and limiting durable therapeutic responses. In addition, T-cell dysfunction and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment further compromise vaccine efficacy. In this review, we discuss the origin and diversity of tumor antigens, recent advances in neoantigen identification and vaccine development, and the biological mechanisms that constrain the clinical success of personalized cancer vaccines. We summarize evidence from clinical trials that highlights both the promise and the current limitations of neoantigen-based immunotherapy, and discuss the importance of incorporating tumor evolution into vaccine design. Finally, we present Variable Epitope Libraries (VELs), a vaccine strategy that uses immunogens based on combinatorial libraries of highly mutated epitope variants designed to broaden immune recognition, reduce immune escape, and improve the durability and effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy.

title: Reframing perineural invasion in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma as a spatial neuroimmune niche
abstract: Perineural invasion (PNI) is an adverse histopathological feature in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), yet its biological meaning is often reduced to a binary pathology variable. This convention overlooks the spatial heterogeneity of the tumour-nerve interface, where nerve subtype, tumour-nerve geometry, stromal organization and immune-cell positioning may carry distinct clinical implications. Recent iCCA-specific evidence identifies, in selected PNI-positive tumours, TH-positive sympathetic fibres, increased norepinephrine, tumour-cell ADRB2-PI3K-AKT-NF-κB-MDK signalling and ferroptosis-associated dysfunction of CD56dimCD16+ natural killer cells. This is currently the strongest disease-specific neuroimmune axis, but it represents only one component of a broader niche that may include CD8+ T-cell exclusion or exhaustion, regulatory and helper T-cell states, macrophage/MDSC suppression, CAF/ECM barriers and TLS topology. In this Review, we distinguish direct iCCA or iCCA-PNI evidence from evidence from other CCA subtypes or general iCCA studies and from cross-cancer hypotheses. We propose a candidate, unvalidated spatial neuroimmune framework that integrates neural phenotyping, spatial immune mapping and imaging. The framework is intended to support four separate research uses-prognostic stratification, preoperative prediction of pathological PNI, pharmacodynamic monitoring and prospective treatment-benefit testing-and should not be treated as a validated clinical score or as a basis for unselected neural or immune therapy. This approach may move PNI reporting from a binary risk label toward a testable, spatially resolved model of iCCA heterogeneity.

title: Co-opted immune homeostatic restraint in Cancer: Mechanisms of immunosuppression and implications for immunotherapy resistance
abstract: Tumors can exploit physiological mechanisms of immune restraint and tissue repair to sustain immunosuppression and limit responses to immunotherapy. This review connects physiological immune regulation with tumor immune escape across checkpoint signaling, metabolism, suppressive immune-cell populations and tissue remodeling. We distinguish activation-coupled negative feedback, persistent deployment of homeostatic or repair programs, and additional tumor-associated suppressive programs, including self-reinforcing circuits. These forms of regulation can coexist and involve shared molecules, but differ in their initiating signals and dependence on continued stimulation or cellular interactions. We examine the evidence linking physiological functions to their altered deployment in cancer and distinguish pre-existing suppression, changes induced during treatment and mechanisms of acquired resistance. We then assess therapeutic strategies according to their experimental and clinical support, including unsuccessful approaches, and discuss how spatial and longitudinal measurements can inform biomarker development and trial design. By linking physiological functions to the processes sustaining suppression, this framework provides a mechanistic basis for classifying immunosuppressive programs. It may guide the selection and timing of therapeutic combinations to achieve more durable antitumor responses.

title: Glioblastoma under chemotherapy pressure: interconnected tumor-cell adaptations shaping tumor behaviour and resistance
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary brain tumor in adults and remains largely incurable because of its marked cellular heterogeneity, limited drug delivery, and rapid development of resistance to temozolomide (TMZ). Beyond its cytotoxic activity, TMZ induces genotoxic and oxidative stress and exerts strong selective pressure, potentially promoting adaptive states in GBM cells that survive chemotherapy. These adaptive responses are heterogeneous and context-dependent and may not only promote tumor cell intrinsic resistance but also strongly reshape the surrounding tumor microenvironment. This review focuses on residual tumor cells that survive TMZ-induced stress and examines how their adaptive responses contribute to treatment resistance and may be sustained by reciprocal interactions with the tumor microenvironment. Specifically, it integrates findings on stem-like enrichment, inflammatory and redox signalling, altered extracellular vesicle release, therapy-induced senescence, and extracellular matrix remodelling, examining how these processes may reinforce one another and link tumor cell survival to signals that influence neighbouring malignant and non-malignant cells. Findings are interpreted within their experimental context, distinguishing evidence from in vitro studies, animal models, and patient samples. This integrated framework provides a rationale for investigating TMZ-based strategies aimed not only at eliminating surviving GBM cells but also at limiting their ability to promote a microenvironment that supports tumor persistence and resistance.
